It organizes control around five checkpoints (pre-action admissibility, action open, assumption capture, approval, outcome closure) and binds them to a portable action envelope carrying authorization, accountability, provenance/externality context, runtime/approval receipts, and replay-ready proof. Evaluated on a protected benchmark (24 seeds expanded to 96 traces across four runtime families), PCAA preserves route quality while ablations expose distinct failure modes.

title: Can Generalist Agents Automate Data Curation?
summary: The paper introduces CURATION-BENCH, an agent-centric benchmark that fixes the model, training recipe, and evaluation suite so a generalist coding agent's only variable is the curated training subset; the agent inspects a candidate data pool, writes a curation policy, submits it through a gated train/eval pipeline (with a contamination audit), and revises across iterations. In vision-language instruction tuning, out-of-the-box agents (Claude Code, Codex, Kimi/Qwen via OpenHands) reach strong published data-selection baselines within ~10 iterations, but trajectory analysis reveals an 'execution-research gap': agents tune local policy variants rather than explore new policy families. Heavy scaffolds that force each iteration to cite, instantiate, and adapt a prior method shift agents toward method-guided exploration, autonomously composing an EL2N-style loss-based selection policy that beats baselines at one-tenth the data budget.

title: LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment
summary: LCSHBench is a multilingual (15-language, 22,346-book), consensus-grounded benchmark for automatically assigning Library of Congress Subject Headings to bibliographic records, built from open Harvard/Columbia/Princeton catalogs where >=2 independent agencies agreed, with released per-catalog provenance and union/unanimous answer views. It defines two tasks (open-vocabulary generation and full-vocabulary retrieval), scores both exact and concept-level matches with set/rank metrics sliced by language and heading type, and motivates a consensus ground truth via a 465K-work inter-cataloger concordance study (93.3% concept agreement vs 39.4% exact). As a demonstration, a sub-dollar LoRA fine-tune of a 300M on-device embedder beats a hosted 3,072-d commercial embedder on exact recall@200, with the gain shown to be specifically cross-lingual.

title: Executable Schema Contracts: From Automatic Ingestion to Multi-Source Retrieval
summary: The paper presents a system that automatically discovers an 'executable schema contract' from raw heterogeneous multi-source data (tables, JSON, docs) and uses it as a shared control plane for both offline knowledge-graph ingestion and query-time retrieval. A closed-world field catalog constrains LLM schema discovery to attested fields, deterministic statistical analysis infers identity/foreign keys and source hierarchy, and the schema drives schema-guided extraction, deduplication, provenance-aware linking, and a multi-tool QA agent that routes across structured lookup, graph traversal, and vector search with traceable citations. In controlled zero-shot QA across four benchmarks it beats RAG and agentic baselines, with ablations showing schema-conditioned routing, structural intelligence, and schema-guided construction each contribute.

title: Data Flow Control: Data Safety Policies for AI Agents
summary: Data Flow Control (DFC) is a framework for declaratively specifying and enforcing data-safety policies (privacy, regulatory, business constraints) over tuple-level data flows inside a DBMS, motivated by AI agents that generate SQL, orchestrate pipelines, and automate analysis where 'correct' queries can still violate governance rules. It formalizes data safety as aggregate predicates over provenance monomials, introduces the PGN declarative policy language, and implements Passant, a query-rewriting layer that enforces policies inline (Full-Push/Partial-Push) without materializing provenance. Across five DBMS engines (DuckDB, Umbra, PostgreSQL, DataFusion, SQLServer) it achieves near-zero overhead and orders-of-magnitude speedups versus provenance-based and LLM-based baselines.

title: TOKI: A Bitemporal Operator Algebra for Contradiction Resolution in LLM-Agent Persistent Memory
summary: TOKI reframes contradiction resolution in LLM-agent persistent memory as write-time concurrency control over a bitemporal, dual-row data substrate. It types the four production resolution heuristics (last-writer-wins, evidence-weighted merge, await-confirmation, per-rule policy) as a single family of bitemporal operators, each carrying an isolation precondition and a K-semiring provenance annotation that preserves the losing fact in an audit row, with soundness theorems closing the contract across isolation, schema, and provenance. A verdict matrix over eight agent-memory systems shows each admits at least one write-time anomaly (replay inconsistency, belief-drift skew, audit erasure) while TOKI excludes all three; on LoCoMo the audit-row defence moves accuracy by +0.86 and ablating the typed memory layer drops accuracy by 0.49 on 1,444 questions.

title: Will the Agent Recuse Itself? Measuring LLM-Agent Compliance with In-Band Access-Deny Signals
summary: The paper proposes the Recuse Signal, a robots.txt-style, in-band, cooperative deny signal that a live server emits over existing protocol channels (SSH banner, PostgreSQL NOTICE, Kubernetes admission webhook) asking an autonomous LLM agent to voluntarily withdraw from a resource. It defines the signal as an open mini-standard, ships three zero/low-footprint adapters, and runs a controlled pilot on a production host showing that compliant agents (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude Code) recuse 100% when the signal is present vs 100% task completion in a no-signal control. The key finding is that compliance is cooperative and model-dependent: an explicit operator-authorization framing flips GPT-4o to proceed, while other agents keep deferring to the on-host policy, treating the resource's own banner as more authoritative than prompt-level authorization.

title: Data Profiling for Change Rules
summary: The paper introduces Change Rules (CRs), a new class of declarative data-quality dependency that bounds sequential changes in both antecedent and consequent attributes over ordered tuples, addressing limits of order/sequential/differential dependencies for trend and causal-change analysis. It proposes CR-Miner, an automated level-wise discovery algorithm using diff-sets and bitset operations, plus a Random Forest context-aware step that learns attribute relevance weights to scale 'abnormal' changes by context. On MIMIC-III, Employment, Weather, and Power datasets it discovers minimal, non-redundant CRs and achieves 40-85% runtime speedups over the FastDD differential-dependency baseline.

title: Traxia: A Framework for Verifiable, Agent-Native Scientific Publishing
summary: Traxia is a proposed agent-native scientific publishing infrastructure in which AI research agents publish 'Verifiable Epistemic Artefacts' (VEAs) that carry cryptographic provenance chains, ordered reasoning traces, confidence intervals, signed agent identities, and append-only reproducibility/contribution logs, organized in a knowledge graph with contradiction detection. The data-management-relevant contributions are its provenance/lineage and metadata-management mechanisms: cryptographically chained version histories, a content-addressed provenance model, immutable replication records, and a living-document staleness score tying artefacts to retracted upstream sources. The paper is architecture and formal specification only (no empirical results); a partial prototype exists and evaluation is deferred to future papers in the series.

title: AgriGov: A Structured Multilingual Dataset Curation for Indian Government Schemes for Farmers
summary: AgriGov is a trilingual (English-Hindi-Marathi) dataset of 50 Indian government farmer-welfare schemes, built through a documented curation pipeline: automated web scraping from official portals, mapping unstructured text into a fixed semantic schema (title, eligibility, application process, documents, exclusions, policy details, source), sentence-level segmentation, placeholder masking of named entities, pivot-based machine translation with selective human post-editing, and heuristic-plus-manual Hindi-Marathi alignment with quality checks. The contribution is a schema-driven, provenance-preserving, version-controlled curation workflow yielding ~2,100 records and ~8,000 aligned sentence pairs for downstream MT, QA, IR, and RAG. It is a data-management/curation pipeline paper (ingest, metadata schema, provenance, data-quality QA) rather than an AI-agent system; automation is conventional scraping and MT, not an autonomous or LLM agent.

title: Trustworthy Smart Fabs via Professional Proxies: Scaling Safe and Sustainable by Design (SSbD) through Industrial Data Spaces
summary: A conceptual zero-trust multi-agent reference architecture ('Professional Proxies') for semiconductor 'Smart Fabs' to operationalize EU sustainability/carbon regulatory compliance (SSbD, CSDDD, CBAM). Role-based agentic workflows (Facility, Process Engineering, Finance proxies) run inside hardware-rooted Trusted Execution Environments, coordinate via a five-step 'relay race', and export cryptographically signed, immutable compliance/provenance tokens (Digital Product Passports) through International Data Spaces connectors and Open-Policy-Agent Policy-as-Code, resolving a 'Data Sovereignty Paradox' (sharing verified compliance data without exposing proprietary process recipes). The work is a Design-Science structural blueprint with no empirical implementation.

title: Automating the Expert Eye: A System-Agnostic Deep Learning Framework for Rare Event Discovery in Imbalanced Force Spectroscopy
summary: The paper presents a deep learning pipeline (a modified ResNet18 with asymmetric Focal Loss, Grad-CAM interpretability, and a dual-threshold triage router) to automate the curation of single-molecule force spectroscopy data, where rare biologically meaningful unbinding events are buried in >90% noise. It tackles the 'data curation crisis' by auto-discarding obvious noise, auto-accepting high-confidence events, and flagging ambiguous traces for human review, cutting manual curation workload by over 90% while preserving 92.31% of rare events. The data-management angle (automated curation / data-quality triage of raw measurement traces) is central, but the approach is classical DL automation in a narrow biophysics domain rather than an LLM/agentic system.

title: Less Context, More Accuracy: A Bi-Temporal Memory Engine for LLM Agents Where a Lean Retrieved Context Beats the Full History
summary: Engram is an open-source memory engine for LLM agents built on a bi-temporal knowledge graph: a fast write path appends lossless episodes, an async path extracts atomic (subject, predicate, object) facts and resolves contradictions by invalidating-not-deleting (preserving full provenance and supersession chains), and a hybrid read path fuses dense/lexical/graph/recency signals with point-in-time 'as-of' filtering to assemble a compact, provenance-tagged context. On LongMemEval_S (500 questions, official judge) the lean ~9.6k-token retrieved slice scores 83.6% vs 73.2% for full-context, beating the full history on accuracy at ~8x fewer tokens. Its provenance, bi-temporal versioning, salience decay, and right-to-be-forgotten/consent design make it relevant to agentic data curation, lineage, and governance.

title: A Five-Plane Reference Architecture for Runtime Governance of Production AI Agents
summary: This paper presents a five-plane reference architecture for runtime governance of production AI agents that read context, call tools, and modify enterprise systems of record. A central reasoning plane adjudicates each proposed agent action against a composite (delegated, capability-attenuated) principal and session state, then projects decisions onto four enforcement planes -- network, identity, endpoint, and data -- where the data plane applies pre-retrieval constraints on classification, residency, retention, and lineage, and a tamper-evident audit substrate produces reconstructible provenance evidence. It contributes a taxonomy of six interruption primitives, four correctness invariants, and a reference policy-engine implementation, demonstrating foreclosure of seven agent threats (e.g. tool-chain exfiltration, connector overreach, audit opacity) across enterprise workflows.

title: An Agentic Retrieval Framework for Autonomous Context-Aware Data Quality Assessment
summary: The paper proposes a unified agentic-retrieval framework that interprets a natural-language description of intended data usage, derives context-aware quality-assessment plans, and generates executable validation logic through a multi-agent workflow (context interpreter, assessment planner, rule generator, feasibility validator, explanation agents), grounded via RAG over a Neo4j knowledge graph of previously validated assessment semantics. A feasibility-validation gate checks generated rules for schema realism and executability before deterministic execution (pandas/DuckDB), separating probabilistic reasoning from auditable scoring. An end-to-end Python prototype is evaluated on the German Credit dataset across business-decision, ML, and regulatory-auditing scenarios, showing that the same dataset yields meaningfully different assessment strategies and scores depending on intended use.

title: Mask-Proof: An LLM-based Automated Data Curation Pipeline on Mathematical Proofs
summary: Mask-Proof is an LLM-based automated data-curation pipeline that ingests recent arXiv math papers (with LaTeX sources), filters/quality-controls proofs, and uses Codex CLI as agents to (i) resolve cross-reference and macro dependencies into self-contained proof contexts and (ii) agentically mask inference-critical formula steps, producing the 292-problem Mask-ProofBench. An LLM equivalence judge (GPT-OSS-120B) with majority voting scores model reconstructions, reaching 96.8% agreement with expert annotators, and the authors run reproducibility, leakage, and ablation studies on the curation steps. The work is fundamentally about agentic curation, quality control, and reproducibility of a curated dataset, with the data-management angle (ingest, dependency/lineage recovery, audit logging) central to the pipeline.

title: PAL-Bench: Evidence-Grounded Profile Reconstruction from Longitudinal Personal Albums
summary: PAL-Bench introduces a controlled benchmark that treats longitudinal personal photo albums as weak-schema multimodal databases and tasks agent systems with reconstructing an owner's profile and social graph by joining faces, OCR text, timestamps, and locations across records, with evidence citation and a privacy-preserving public/private separation. An Evidence Compiler builds latent private worlds, programs evidence paths, renders pixels, and re-measures them through perception pipelines so the evaluator holds complete ground truth while agents see only perception-derived public records. Across seven system classes (heuristic, text-only LLM, multimodal RAG, long-context LLM, tool-use agents, lifelog baseline) plus the reference PAL-TRACE framework, no system solves the task: systems summarize owner facts plausibly but fail at recurring-identity binding and faithful provenance citation.

title: SkillWiki: A Living Knowledge Infrastructure for Agent Skills
summary: SkillWiki is a demonstration of a 'living knowledge infrastructure' that manages the full lifecycle of LLM agent skills: ingesting heterogeneous knowledge sources (trajectories, docs, API specs, scripts, historical skills), producing governed skill assets, tracking provenance/lineage via a heterogeneous Skill Provenance Graph, and supporting Git-style governance, versioning, health monitoring, and execution-driven evolution. It is evaluated via a 125-artifact knowledge-to-skill production benchmark (99 converted to governed skills) and a full-chain lifecycle case study across states S0-S7. While framed around agent skills rather than data assets, it directly applies data-management concepts (curation, metadata/manifests, provenance, governance/compliance, quality/health) to those skills.

title: An Evaluation of Data Leakage Risks in Tool-Using LLM Agents in Realistic Scenarios
summary: A joint Singapore-Korea AI Safety Institute evaluation measures data leakage by tool-using LLM agents in 12 realistic, non-adversarial enterprise/personal tasks (HR onboarding, customer support, DevOps, web automation), scored against five risk types: data awareness, audience awareness, policy compliance, data minimization, and access-boundary awareness. Across three agent models none achieved fully correct and fully safe execution; successful task completion often coincided with leaking unnecessary or misdirected sensitive data, showing capability and data-handling safety must be evaluated separately. It contributes a reusable evaluation methodology (ReAct scaffolds, MCP tool environments, simulated user LLMs, task-specific LLM-judge rubrics) and surfaces failure modes like claim-action mismatch, hallucinated data, and simulation-aware behavior.

title: Lifetime Sample Tracking (LiST): A Data Platform for Materials Science
summary: LiST (Lifetime Sample Tracking) is a deployed data-management and analysis platform built by Penn State's 2DCC-MIP national user facility to automatically capture, curate, share, and preserve the full lifecycle of materials-synthesis data (~20,000 samples across MBE, MOCVD, bulk growth, plus characterization like AFM, RHEED, Raman, XRD). It uses lab 'Gatekeeper' servers and Microsoft Graph notifications to automate ingest into SQL/cloud storage, enforces standardized sample IDs and naming, flags incomplete/mislabeled data for review, and provides FAIR provenance via DOI-stamped Data Packages (ScholarSphere) and instrument PIDs (DMR-FIRST), exposed through a REST API. Downstream it enables ML analyses (CNN transfer-learning classification, segmentation/regression, UMAP/PCA, generative cross-modal models) and aims toward future autonomous synthesis.

title: Trustworthy Self-Composable Big-Data-as-a-Service: An LLM-Orchestrated Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Data Engineering, AutoML, MLOps Deployment, and Drift
summary: The paper proposes a trustworthy self-composable Big-Data-as-a-Service (BDaaS) framework in which a central LLM orchestrator coordinates specialized agents for data ingestion, cleaning, feature engineering, AutoML training, evaluation, MLOps deployment, and drift monitoring, layered over a shared artifact-governance store for metadata, versioning, lineage and reproducibility. A prototype is evaluated on controlled tabular benchmarks (with missing values, outliers, class imbalance, and injected covariate drift) against manual ML, AutoML-only, and single-agent LLM baselines. The multi-agent pipeline matches or slightly beats baselines on predictive accuracy while substantially improving lifecycle reliability metrics (100% workflow completion, artifact traceability, deployment readiness, reproducibility) and recovering from injected drift within one monitoring window.

title: ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents
summary: ProvenanceGuard is a source-aware factuality verifier for tool-using (MCP) LLM agents that, unlike source-blind support checks, verifies not only whether a claim is supported but whether it is attributed to the correct evidence source (catching 'cross-source conflation'). It decomposes answers into atomic claims, routes each to source-specific MCP evidence via embeddings, checks support with NLI plus token-alignment, applies a random-forest calibrator, separately checks stated-vs-routed attribution, and blocks/repairs answers; on 281 medical MCP-agent traces it reaches block F1 0.802 and source accuracy 0.858, and detects all 50 injected attribution swaps. The work frames source attribution as an independent axis of factuality/provenance verification for agentic, multi-tool data settings.

title: RedactionBench
summary: RedactionBench is a manually annotated benchmark of 200 documents across 11 domains for PII redaction, framed as a data-cleaning prerequisite and grounded in contextual integrity (whether information is sensitive depends on who holds it and why). It introduces R-Score, a character-level metric that rewards partial overlap and ignores formatting differences, and evaluates 35 models including NER models, small language models, and frontier LLMs equipped with agentic file-editing tool calls. Frontier agentic models top the leaderboard (R-Score 0.71 overall, 0.81 on the user-study split, exceeding the human baseline of 0.77), but contextual redaction remains unsolved and humans disagree sharply on context-dependent cases (only 47.7% agreement).

title: GateMem: Benchmarking Memory Governance in Multi-Principal Shared-Memory Agents
summary: GateMem is a benchmark for evaluating memory governance in multi-principal shared-memory LLM agents (hospitals, offices, campuses, households), jointly measuring utility for legitimate queries, access control across role/scope/relationship boundaries, and active forgetting after explicit deletion requests. Across 91 episodes and 2,218 hidden checkpoints in four domains, no baseline (long-context, RAG, or dedicated memory systems like A-Mem/Mem0/ReMem) simultaneously achieves strong utility, robust access control, and reliable forgetting; long-context scores best on governance but at high token cost and still leaks. The work frames shared agent memory as a governed data state requiring authorization enforcement and deletion semantics, not just recall.

title: Runtime Compliance Verification for AI Agents
summary: C-Trace is a runtime verification framework that enforces GDPR compliance on tool-using AI agents by encoding four principles (consent, purpose limitation, data minimization, right to erasure) as first-order predicates over the agent's typed execution trace, with an in-process interceptor that monitors every tool call/model output and blocks non-compliant actions. The same policy is expressed in three runtimes (operational Python monitor, auditor-facing Rego/OPA, and MFOTL specs replayable by MonPoly) that cross-validate, and it is evaluated against an adversarial attack driver across four GDPR-reframed case studies. Under exact extraction the monitor reaches 0% attack-success and 0% false positives; under 10% extractor noise it keeps ASR <=12% and FPR <=16%, with the category extractor identified as the main failure mode.

title: Deontic Policies for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems
summary: The paper proposes AgenticRei, a runtime governance layer that enforces deontic policies (permissions, prohibitions, obligations, dispensations, and meta-policy conflict resolution) on agent tool-calls and agent-to-agent messages, evaluated deterministically outside the LLM via an OWL/RDF (Rei) policy engine on RDFox. Several worked examples directly govern data-management actions, prohibiting export of regulated datasets, blocking reads of Protected Health Information via ontological subclass reasoning, and gating data access on trusted-issuer credentials, mapping to data governance, access control, and compliance. It argues flat allow/deny engines (XACML, Rego, Cedar) cannot express obligation lifecycles, ontology-grounded constraints, or named meta-policy conflict resolution, and reports sub-10ms per-decision latency.

title: How to spot outliers: an Ensemble Anomaly Detection Framework
summary: The paper proposes EQAF (Ensemble Quality Assessment Framework), a layered unsupervised pipeline that monitors the integrity and data quality of investment-bank risk-calculation outputs (PV, P&L, credit deltas) in real time. It combines six statistical/ML detectors (Robust Z-Score, ECDF scoring, Hampel filter, Rolling Z-Score, Isolation Forest, LOF) with ECDF score normalization, weighted majority-vote aggregation, and a deterministic stale-value override, evaluated via a controlled anomaly-injection protocol on proprietary UBS credit-derivatives data. The ensemble reaches F1 of 61-79%, beats the best single method, and shows that frozen-feed (stale-value) errors require deterministic domain rules since purely statistical methods get 0% recall on them.

title: DEMM-Bench: A Cross-Regime Benchmark for Agent-Runtime Governance-Evidence Sufficiency
summary: DEMM-Bench is a cross-regime benchmark that measures whether the heterogeneous evidence an AI agent runtime emits (traces, signed ledgers, W3C-style provenance graphs, delegation tokens, policy logs, lifecycle audit trails) is actually sufficient to reconstruct decision-level governance properties — actor, authority, action, policy basis, decision basis, resource touch, lifecycle context, verification strength — rather than merely present. Grounded in the Decision Evidence Maturity Model, it normalizes eight evidence regimes through adapters, applies eight deterministic degradation conditions over 64 synthetic cases, and shows that container-presence baselines (trace/schema/ledger-present) overclaim sufficiency on 50-75% of cases while a redacted property-level scorer has zero overclaim at 56.25% mean Property Sufficiency Accuracy. It targets the gap between observability-grade and accountability-grade evidence for governing autonomous-agent decisions.

title: Building Agent Harnesses for Scientific Curation from Multimodal Sources
summary: Beaver is an agent harness for scientific curation: it extracts schema-constrained structured records from full multimodal papers (text, tables, figures) while preserving provenance traces linking each value back to supporting evidence. It combines a frontier base agent with multimodal evidence tooling, staged task scaffolding, and an artifact-grounded autoresearch loop that iteratively diagnoses stage-localized failures and revises the harness, reaching 81.0 GRAS versus 58.6 for the best off-the-shelf baseline. The work shows that for curation from papers, harness design (not just base-model strength) is the central performance determinant, with the largest gains on attributes needing cross-modal reasoning and normalization.

title: Towards Imputation of Pre-Trained Language Model Metadata using Semantic Fingerprinting
summary: SemFin (Semantic Fingerprinting) is a lightweight, artifact-driven method that automatically imputes missing Hugging Face model metadata (license, reuse method, pipeline tag, model type, training library) and reconstructs model lineage by fusing config.json configuration keys with repository tags, trained as ML classifiers over 317,133 PTLMs. It outperforms graph-propagation baselines (Graph Avg / Hub Avg) by up to ~31% accuracy, covers isolated models the baselines cannot, and when applied at scale expands traceable reuse-method and license lineage chains by ~76% and ~54%, exposing previously invisible reuse patterns and hidden license incompatibilities. The work positions automatically derived structural signals as the foundation for automated AI Bills of Materials (AIBOMs), shifting metadata from error-prone manual declaration to inference from model artifacts.

title: Harness-MU: A Safe, Governed, and Effective Harness for Multi-User LLM Agents
summary: Harness-MU is a model-agnostic, zero-tuning runtime harness for multi-user LLM agents that moves data-governance constraints (who is authorized, what is restricted, whose instructions take precedence) out of the probabilistic LLM and into deterministic execution hooks across four decoupled modules (Gatekeeper, Mediator, isolated per-user Workers, ComplianceChecker). On the Muses-Bench multi-principal benchmark across four frontier models, it guarantees zero unauthorized leakage (privacy=1.000) while improving utility by 0.28-0.39 and instruction-following accuracy by up to 48.9 points over the prompt-based baseline. The work argues that deterministic 'Harness Engineering' infrastructure, not better prompting, is what reliably solves access control and authoritative-conflict resolution for collaborative agents.

title: VISTA Architect: A graph database-oriented health AI system demonstrated in multidisciplinary tumor boards
summary: VISTA Architect is a database-oriented health AI system that, at ingestion, transforms longitudinal EHR documentation into a persistent, provenance-linked knowledge graph: a source-faithful MEDS Graph plus a clinically abstracted Timeline Object Architecture (TOA) built via graph-guided LLM extraction that deduplicates and temporally reconciles clinical events. An agentic AI bridge then navigates this precomputed graph (traversing to source documents only for verification) rather than re-processing raw records per query, addressing cost, latency, and temporal-fidelity limits of long-context prompting and RAG. Demonstrated on 1,180 Stanford thoracic-oncology tumor-board patients, it reached 96.4% extraction accuracy on 15 salient variables, beat a BM25 RAG baseline by ~30 points, and cut case prep to ~2.2 minutes via parallelized agentic processing.

title: Intent-Governed Tool Authorization for AI Agents
summary: The paper proposes Intent-Governed Access Control (IGAC), a server-side authorization layer that binds an AI agent's tool calls to the user's expressed intent, so that intent can only narrow (never widen) the static integration authority over data operations like reading, exporting, updating, or deleting records. IGAC introduces intent certificates, session-scoped policy narrowing, intent-aware tool-manifest filtering, intent-tool-payload consistency checks, and audit binding, layered on top of the OpenPort governance substrate (draft-first writes, preflight impact hashing, idempotency, stable reason codes, audit). Evaluation is mechanism- and runtime-path level: deterministic endpoint tests, a 176-task synthetic microbenchmark, a real-LLM classifier/planner pilot, and small/external-subset end-to-end LLM runtime pilots, with explicit non-claims about deployment-level robustness.

title: Governed Shared Memory for Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: The paper reframes shared memory for fleets of cooperating LLM agents as a governed distributed-data problem rather than a retrieval problem, formalizing a fleet-memory model (agents, memory substrate, governance, provenance, temporal supersession) and four failure modes: unauthorized leakage, stale propagation, contradiction persistence, and provenance collapse. It implements scoped retrieval, temporal supersession, provenance tracking, and policy-governed propagation in a production multi-tenant service (MemClaw) and evaluates them live via an open harness (ArgusFleet) across four governance dimensions. Live measurement surfaced two real production defects — a sub-tenant scope bypass on the GET-by-id path (since remediated) and a synchronous near-duplicate gate that pre-empts asynchronous contradiction detection — arguing that long-context retrieval alone is insufficient for governed multi-agent memory.

title: Research Data Preservation Using Process Engines and Machine-Actionable Data Management Plans
summary: This paper (LNCS 2018) describes using business-process/workflow engines together with machine-actionable Data Management Plans (maDMPs) to automate research data preservation. The maDMP encodes preservation requirements in a machine-readable form so a process engine can execute the corresponding preservation actions, reducing manual effort in the data-management lifecycle. It is classical, standards-driven automation (maDMP + process orchestration) rather than an LLM/AI-agent system, but it directly targets DMP-based planning and preservation/curation.

title: Understanding RegTech for Digital Regulatory Compliance
summary: This 2018 book chapter examines RegTech for digital regulatory compliance in finance, arguing that the industry's 'Tower of Babel' (lack of a common language across siloed systems) is the core obstacle, solvable only via open semantic standards. It reports on the Bank of England/FCA RegTech Sprint, where AI/NLP plus W3C semantic technologies (SKOS taxonomies, SBVR/RDF rules in the SmaRT tool, OWL ontologies, SPARQL) were used to tag regulations, transform legalese into human- and machine-readable rules, and enable straight-through, semi-automated regulatory reporting (e.g., FSA001 balance sheet from Santander customer data). It positions enterprise data management, governance, and semantic interoperability as the central lens for RegTech, with provenance from regulation to code as a key requirement.

title: Machine-Actionable Data Management Plans: A Knowledge Retrieval Approach to Automate the Assessment of Funders’ Requirements
summary: This paper addresses machine-actionable Data Management Plans (maDMPs), proposing a knowledge retrieval approach to automatically assess whether a DMP meets funders' requirements. It targets the data-management planning and compliance/governance stage, where checking conformance to funder mandates is otherwise manual. Only title-level metadata is available (no abstract or PDF), so solution and evaluation details are inferred from the title and venue.

title: Extracting Provenance of Machine Learning Experiment Pipeline Artifacts
summary: This paper (Schlegel & Sattler, ADBIS 2023) proposes a W3C PROV-compliant provenance model that captures the provenance of machine-learning experiment pipelines and their artifacts in terms of Git and MLflow activities. It introduces MLflow2PROV, a tool that automatically extracts provenance graphs from existing ML projects so the captured pipeline provenance can be queried, analyzed, and further processed for reproducibility and lineage. The work targets the provenance/lineage stage of the data/ML lifecycle via automated extraction rather than an AI agent.

title: A W3C PROV–Aligned Metamodel for Tracing End-to-End Provenance in ML Pipelines
summary: This paper proposes a W3C PROV-aligned metamodel for tracing end-to-end provenance across machine-learning pipelines, addressing the data-management need to capture lineage from raw data through model training and deployment. Only the title is available (no abstract or PDF), so the solution architecture, evaluation, and findings could not be verified. The provenance/lineage focus and standards alignment place it within data-management scope, though whether it employs AI agents versus classical metadata automation is unknown.

title: ProvAbs: Model, Policy, and Tooling for Abstracting PROV Graphs
summary: ProvAbs presents a formal Provenance Abstraction Model centered on a 'Group' operator that replaces a set of nodes in a W3C PROV graph with a single abstract node while preserving graph validity (no type-constraint violations, no new relations, no new usage-generation cycles), via closure/extension/replacement. It adds a simple policy language so data owners ('Policy Setters') annotate nodes with sensitivity/utility values and auto-generate grouping sets per receiver clearance level (Bell-LaPadula style), with a residual-utility metric to quantify information loss. The ProvAbs tool implements this over a Neo4J graph database (Cypher + Traverse API) and was demonstrated on a confidentiality-preserving intelligence-information-exchange use case.

title: Generating Scientific Documentation for Computational Experiments Using Provenance
summary: This 2015 paper proposes automatically generating human-readable scientific documentation for computational experiments by leveraging provenance information captured during execution. It targets the provenance/lineage and metadata-documentation stages of the data lifecycle, reducing the manual burden of describing how results were produced. (Assessed from title/metadata only; no abstract or full text was available.)

title: Walking into the Future with PROV Pingback: An Application to OPeNDAP Using Prizms
summary: This 2015 paper develops the W3C PROV Pingback technique and couples it minimally to the Prizms Linked Data platform so existing host systems (demonstrated on the OPeNDAP Earth-science data transport server) can publish and interconnect provenance records with little effort. It lets downstream clients report derivations of served data back to the host, aggregating structural and behavioral provenance into discoverable Linked Data. The contribution is reducing the cost of adding provenance while increasing its value by linking otherwise-isolated records.

title: LabelFlow: Exploiting Workflow Provenance to Surface Scientific Data Provenance
summary: LabelFlow is a semi-automated infrastructure that exploits generic scientific-workflow provenance to surface domain-specific scientific data provenance by attaching propagatable 'Data Labels' to data artefacts. It annotates workflow activities with reusable 'Motif' types (Data Minting vs Data Preparation/value-copying), then compiles 'Labelling Pipelines' from four operators (Mint, Propagate, Distribute, Generalize) that mint and propagate labels across workflow runs, improving the contextual precision of data-selection/scoping queries over plain lineage traversal. Evaluated on an astronomy galaxy-extinction workflow, label-based queries beat lineage-based ones except where black-box steps (e.g. Flatten_List) destroy fine-grained traceability.

title: Automating Electronic Health Record Data Quality Assessment
summary: This PRISMA-ScR scoping review (1841 articles screened, 23 included) surveys software programs and toolkits that automate Electronic Health Record data quality assessment (DQA), covering both real-world deployments (n=14) and experimental prototypes (n=9). It distills 24 design features into a five-category conceptual model (DQ-Task, DQ-Measurement, Target-Data, DQ-Report, DQ-Mechanism) and a UML schema for operationalising EHR DQA. It finds automation is gaining traction but efforts are fragmented, focused on easy dimensions (completeness, value conformance), tightly coupled to local infrastructure, and rarely grounded in DQ theory.

title: Automated Metadata Suggestion During Repository Submission
summary: This Neuroinformatics paper presents a system that automatically suggests metadata to researchers as they submit datasets to a (neuroimaging) data repository, reducing the manual annotation burden and improving metadata completeness/quality at ingest time. The approach targets the curation/metadata stage of the data-management lifecycle by proposing field values during submission. Full text and abstract were unavailable, so the assessment is based on title and venue.

title: Black Swan Events and Intelligent Automation for Routine Safety Surveillance
summary: This Current Opinion argues for trusted intelligent automation (robotic process automation combined with machine learning) in the data-ingestion and processing stages of pharmacovigilance safety surveillance, focusing on how such automated pipelines can still robustly detect and triage rare, unexpected 'black swan' safety events rather than smoothing them away as noise. It outlines design strategies for ML-enabled data intake -- data-drift monitoring with significant-change triggers for human review, out-of-distribution/anomaly detection, ensemble and orthogonal data mining, current metadata, uncertainty estimates and 'requires human review' outputs, and privacy-preserving processing. It is a perspective/argument piece (with illustrative case tables) rather than a built or benchmarked agent system.

title: A large-scale evaluation of automated metadata inference approaches on sensors from air handling units
summary: A large-scale empirical study evaluating six time-series-based automated metadata inference approaches that classify building sensor points (e.g., discharge/return air temperature, valve commands) into a consistent schema (Brick) so that portable building applications can be deployed without manual metadata curation. Tested on 614 air handling units across 421 buildings and 35 sites, it benchmarks accuracy across sites, training-data regimes, and temporal/spatial splits, finding Random Forest best (~78%) and significant per-site variance. It frames metadata inference as the way to semi-automatically standardize legacy building metadata at scale.

title: Medical data quality assessment: On the development of an automated framework for medical data curation
summary: This 2019 paper presents an automated framework for assessing medical data quality and supporting medical data curation. It targets the data-quality/curation stage of the data-management lifecycle, applying automation to evaluate and clean medical datasets. Assessment is metadata-only (no abstract or PDF available), and the work predates LLM-based agents, representing classical rule/metric-driven automation rather than agentic AI.

title: Globus automation services: Research process automation across the space–time continuum
summary: Describes Globus automation services, which let researchers specify reusable sets of actions ('flows') and execute them across heterogeneous, distributed research resources (instruments, compute, data stores) within the Globus research data management platform. Key features include reliable cloud hosting of long-lived flows, an extensible asynchronous action-provider API, an event-driven execution model, and a delegation-based security model for secure long-running cross-resource actions. It is classical workflow/process automation for the data-management lifecycle rather than AI- or LLM-based agents.

title: Semantic agent framework for automated flood assessment using dynamic knowledge graphs
summary: The paper proposes a framework of linked autonomous software agents operating over the World Avatar dynamic knowledge graph to continuously ingest and semantically integrate fragmented real-time environmental, flood, building, and population data, then automatically re-assess flood impact. Three new OWL ontologies (OntoEMS, OntoFlood, OntoBuiltEnv) model and link the domains, while a Derived Information Framework (DIF) tracks data provenance/dependencies and cascades updates so that new flood warnings automatically trigger re-evaluation of people and building stock at risk. It is demonstrated as a deployed digital-twin use case for King's Lynn, UK.

title: Tracking materials science data lineage to manage millions of materials experiments and analyses
summary: The paper presents MEAD, a lightweight data-management framework that tracks data lineage and metadata across the synthesis, measurement, association, analysis, and exploration phases of high-throughput materials experiments, yielding a searchable database of millions of experiments. It uses read-only file conventions, automated ingestion/metadata extraction, a relational database for referential integrity, and versioned links to analysis code to maintain full provenance and FAIR compliance. While framed around enabling automation and autonomous discovery, the system itself is classical scripted data-pipeline automation rather than AI agents.

title: Evaluating FAIR maturity through a scalable, automated, community-governed framework
summary: The paper presents the FAIR Evaluator, a scalable, community-governed framework for automatically assessing the FAIRness of digital resources. Given only a resource's GUID, an automated agent (Metadata Harvester plus per-indicator Compliance Tests) autonomously resolves, harvests, and interprets (meta)data over the Web, returning a transparent pass/fail report that doubles as a roadmap for improving FAIR maturity. Maturity Indicators and test collections are authored and bundled by communities, making assessments domain-relevant, versioned, reusable, and themselves FAIR.

title: Lightweight Distributed Provenance Model for Complex Real–world Environments
summary: This paper introduces a 'provenance backbone' — a lightweight W3C PROV-based model for building distributed provenance (lineage) chains across multiple organizations, with connectors, harmonized derivation paths, jump connectors for missing links, bundle versioning, and a uniform traversal algorithm. It is demonstrated on a real-world digital-pathology pipeline (specimen acquisition through AI tumor-detection model training/testing), with automated provenance generation implemented for the computational steps (WSI preprocessing, training, testing). The model became the conceptual foundation of the ISO 23494 biotechnology provenance standard. The AI model here is the object whose lineage is tracked rather than an agent performing data management, and the automation is conventional log-to-PROV translation.

title: An agentic AI framework for ingestion and standardization of single-cell RNA-seq data analysis
summary: CellAtria is a LangGraph-based, multi-actor agentic AI framework that turns a single high-level natural-language instruction (e.g., an article URL) into an end-to-end scRNA-seq data-reuse workflow: it parses primary literature (web or local PDF), extracts structured metadata (species, tissue, accession IDs), retrieves datasets from public repositories (GEO at study or sample level), organizes files in the workspace, and dispatches a co-developed standardized analysis pipeline (CellExpress). It deliberately avoids ad-hoc LLM code generation in favor of orchestrating a library of pre-vetted, schema-validated tools, with interactive panels (log viewer, terminal, file browser) and exportable transcripts/metadata for transparency, auditability, and GxP-style reproducibility. Benchmarked across 25 public datasets (290 samples) and an autonomous run completing in ~10 min vs ~15 hours of manual effort, it emphasizes human-in-the-loop oversight and harmonized metadata/repository annotations as future needs.

title: PubTator central: automated concept annotation for biomedical full text articles
summary: PubTator Central is a web service that applies automated text-mining systems to annotate biomedical concepts (genes/proteins, variants, diseases, chemicals, species, cell lines) across ~29M PubMed abstracts and ~3M PMC full-text articles, with a deep-learning disambiguation module to improve accuracy. Annotations are downloadable in XML/JSON/tab-delimited formats via web UI, REST API, and FTP, explicitly to support biocuration, gene prioritization, and literature-based knowledge discovery. It is automated metadata/concept extraction and curation support, but classical NLP pipelines rather than an agentic system.

title: scBaseCount: an AI agent-curated, uniformly processed, and autonomously updated single cell data repository
summary: scBaseCount uses an AI agent to mine all 10x Genomics single-cell RNA-seq datasets from the SRA, automatically discovering datasets, extracting and standardizing their unstructured metadata, and uniformly reprocessing the reads. The result is the largest freely accessible public single-cell repository (>502M cells across 27 organisms and 75 tissues) that the agent can autonomously keep updated. The authors frame it as a blueprint for AI-driven curation and continuous maintenance of large biological data repositories.

title: FLAG-PDFe: Features Oriented Metadata Extraction Framework for Scientific Publications
summary: FLAG-PDFe is a four-stage framework that automatically extracts metadata (authors, affiliations, country, sections, tables/figures, supplementary material, funding agencies, EU projects) from scientific publication PDFs. It first recovers physical layout (font/geometric properties, column style, reading order), engineers distinct and generic features, uses SVM (SVC) to classify logical layout structure, and applies heuristics on that structure to extract the target metadata. On the ESWC SemPub gold-standard dataset it reaches 0.877 recall / 0.928 precision / 0.897 F-measure, a 16% F-measure gain over the SemPub2016 challenge winner.

title: Understanding Scanner Utilization With Real-Time DICOM Metadata Extraction
summary: Niffler is an open-source framework that transfers DICOM images from a hospital PACS into a research cluster in real time, automatically extracts a configurable subset of metadata headers into a MongoDB store, and runs algorithms to compute radiology scanner utilization metrics (study duration, encounters, multi-exam grouping). It addresses the lack of scalable, automated DICOM metadata extraction in hospitals, which otherwise rely on error-prone manually-entered RIS records. Benchmarks over 28 days across 25 MRI scanners show the PACS-metadata approach more accurately captures scanner utilization and multi-exam encounters than RIS, though it under-counts studies with zero/missing-header images.

title: Efficient Automated Processing of the Unstructured Documents Using Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Literature Review and Future Directions
summary: A Systematic Literature Review (Kitchenham/Charters, 83 primary studies, 2010-2020) of AI-based techniques for automatically extracting information from unstructured documents such as invoices, receipts, EHRs, and contracts. It compares OCR, Robotics Process Automation (including cognitive RPA), and NER/ML/deep-learning approaches, surveys publicly available datasets and their quality issues, and identifies the lack of data validation techniques and high-quality real-world datasets as key gaps. It concludes by conceptualizing a framework for building high-quality unstructured-document datasets with strong data validation to support automated extraction.

title: Framing the scope of the common data model for machine-actionable Data Management Plans
summary: This paper reports the RDA DMP Common Standards working group's effort to frame the scope of a common data model for machine-actionable Data Management Plans (maDMPs), moving beyond static, manually-implemented text DMPs toward plans that systems can act on. Through stakeholder consultations and proof-of-concept tools, it identifies stakeholder information needs, defines the data model scope for inter-system information exchange, and enumerates the services/infrastructure components needed to automate data management tasks. It is a standards/architecture contribution enabling automated, scalable DM rather than an AI-agent implementation.

title: Can Automated Metadata Extraction Make Scientific Data More Navigable?
summary: This e-Science 2023 paper evaluates whether automatically extracted metadata makes scientific data repositories more navigable, using the Xtract metadata extraction system to build searchable indexes over data files at two U.S. national labs (spectroscopy and battery-modeling projects). A two-part user study first identified scientists' navigation needs (discovery, retrieval, organization), then had participants complete simulated navigation tasks; auto-built indexes let users solve tasks with high confidence/correctness and 1.2X-50X faster than manual directory scans or custom tools. The work is automation-centric (scalable parsing of nonstandard schemas) rather than agentic, but addresses the metadata-extraction stage of data management directly.

title: Skluma: An Extensible Metadata Extraction Pipeline for Disorganized Data
summary: Skluma is a system that automatically crawls a target filesystem or repository, classifies file types with machine learning, then dynamically prioritizes and runs a suite of pluggable extractors to derive content- and context-based metadata (aggregate values, named entities, latent topics, image content), emitted as probabilistic JSON for downstream discovery and organization. It runs locally or as an on-demand cloud service, is modular and user-extensible, and was demonstrated on a 500,000+-file environmental science repository at modest cost. The work targets the metadata-curation stage of the data-management lifecycle via classical pipeline automation rather than an LLM agent.

title: Automated metadata extraction: challenges and opportunities
summary: This paper examines automated metadata extraction systems that crawl data repositories and orchestrate lightweight 'extractors' to mine FAIR-aligned metadata with minimal human effort, grounded in the authors' Xtract system (a FaaS-based extractor that has processed >500M files across climate, battery, spectroscopy, and materials data). It defines the extraction problem (isolate/select/apply/rate methods plus quality metrics like completeness, correctness, relevance) and surfaces three core challenges: divergent and conflicting data-consumer perspectives, evolving metadata standards/ontologies, and growth of the extractor library causing redundant compute. It proposes 'microextractors' (finer, composable, dependency-graphed extraction functions with checkpointed state) and multi-context/subjective metadata views as research directions.

title: PROV-AGENT: Unified Provenance for Tracking AI Agent Interactions in Agentic Workflows
summary: PROV-AGENT extends the W3C PROV standard to capture agent-centric metadata (prompts, responses, decisions) and link it to end-to-end workflow provenance, using the Model Context Protocol and data observability. The goal is to make AI-agent actions transparent, traceable, reproducible, and reliable so hallucination risks and error propagation across agents can be assessed and mitigated. It is evaluated across edge, cloud, and HPC environments to support provenance queries and agent reliability analysis.

title: An Automated Metadata Generation Method for Data Lake of Industrial WoT Applications
summary: The paper proposes an automated bottom-up metadata generation method for data lakes serving industrial Web of Things (WoT) applications, where heterogeneous, weakly-described streaming data make manual metadata modeling infeasible. A data-driven pipeline annotates raw data as linked data, uses self-organizing-map online clustering to extract data characteristics in real time, applies a semantics-based entity discovery approach for short texts, and performs numerical analysis to surface hidden relations, ultimately constructing full-dimensional semantic metadata. It is validated on a real-world dataset plus an energy WoT system case study.

title: Combining User Reputation and Provenance Analysis for Trust Assessment
summary: This 2016 paper presents an automated pipeline that estimates the trustworthiness of data artifacts from their W3C PROV provenance combined with user reputation, using stereotype generation and subjective-logic evidential reasoning. It extracts provenance features, derives user-behavior stereotypes, estimates reputations, and selects trustworthy artifacts, achieving up to 85% precision on the Waisda? video-tagging and Steve.Museum crowdsourced datasets. It is a classical algorithmic data-quality/provenance pipeline rather than an LLM/agent-based system.

title: Automated Quality Assessment of Metadata across Open Data Portals
summary: This 2016 paper presents a generic, automatable framework for assessing metadata quality across Open Data portals by mapping the metadata of three portal software frameworks (CKAN, Socrata, OpenDataSoft) to the standardized DCAT vocabulary and defining several efficiently computable quality metrics. The authors apply it to a monitored corpus of over 260 portals with 1.1M datasets, reporting issues such as data retrievability and per-metric quality gaps. The work targets searchability, discoverability, and usability of open data through scalable, automated quality monitoring rather than via LLM/AI agents.

title: On Automating Basic Data Curation Tasks
summary: This 2017 paper identifies and implements a set of 'basic data curation APIs' exposed as open-source REST/JSON services to automate transforming raw data into curated, contextualized data. The services cover named-entity extraction, POS tagging, keyword extraction, synonym/stemming via WordNet, entity linking to Google Knowledge Graph and Wikidata, similarity computation, classification/categorization, and indexing of structured and unstructured data. It is classical automation tooling for the curation lifecycle stage rather than an autonomous agent.

title: A Serverless Framework for Distributed Bulk Metadata Extraction
summary: Xtract is an automated, scalable system for bulk metadata extraction from large, distributed research data repositories. It orchestrates container-based metadata extractors over a federated FaaS platform (funcX), deciding which extractors to apply to each file and where to run them to balance extraction time against data-transfer cost. Demonstrated on multi-million-file repositories across clouds and supercomputers, it processes large collections in ~50% of the time needed just to transfer the data to a central machine.

title: Automating Research Data Management Using Machine-Actionable Data Management Plans
summary: The paper describes a system for machine-actionable data management plans (maDMPs) that semi-automates the creation and maintenance of DMPs within an institutional research data management infrastructure. It proposes a reference architecture, identifies automatable use cases, and evaluates how far EC and national-funder DMP templates can be pre-filled in a case study at a large Austrian technical university. It is classical-automation/interoperability driven (RDA maDMP standard) rather than an LLM-agent system, but is directly about automating DM planning, metadata integration, and updates.

title: Machine Learning and Data Cleaning: Which Serves the Other?
summary: A vision/discussion article in the Journal of Data and Information Quality examining the symbiotic, dual relationship between machine learning and data cleaning: 'ML for automating data cleaning/preparation' and 'data cleaning for ML'. It argues that automated/semi-automated data quality, cleaning, and integration systems increasingly rely on ML, while ML deployments depend heavily on input data quality, and calls for collaboration across research communities to address the resulting challenges. No system, agent architecture, or empirical evaluation is presented (assessed from abstract only).

title: MLflow2PROV: Extracting Provenance from Machine Learning Experiments
summary: MLflow2PROV proposes a W3C-PROV-compliant provenance model and a tool that extracts provenance graphs from Git history and MLflow experiment-management usage, addressing the limited provenance capabilities of ML experiment management systems. The extracted graphs enable querying, analysis, and downstream processing of provenance to improve ML models and development workflows. It is squarely a provenance/lineage data-management contribution but is deterministic tooling rather than an AI/LLM agent.

title: Conceptual service architecture to synchronise research data management services using machine-actionable data management plans
summary: This paper proposes a conceptual service architecture that uses machine-actionable data management plans (maDMPs) to automatically exchange and synchronize information among semi-automated research data management services acting on behalf of different stakeholders, so DMPs stay up to date across the research lifecycle. The authors derive requirements from change use cases, model the architecture via UML and BPMN views, and instantiate it by connecting a data repository to a DMP tool. The work aims to advance the RDA's maDMP recommendation and improve interconnectivity across planning, tracking, and assessing research phases.

title: Quality Dimensions and Evaluation Framework for Machine-Actionable DMPs
summary: This article presents a conceptual framework and prototype for automatically evaluating machine-actionable Data Management Plans (maDMPs), replacing the labor-intensive manual review process. It contributes a taxonomy of evaluation goals/dimensions with metrics, a DMP Quality Vocabulary (DMPQV) for standardized quality communication, and a mechanism for contextual information, validated via a case study against the Science Europe Practical Guide. The work targets FAIR assessment and funder compliance, generating standardized quality reports that align with manual assessments.

title: Data Management Planning: How Requirements and Solutions are Beginning to Converge
summary: This opinion/review article surveys the state of data management planning (DMP) tools (DMPonline, DMPTool, DMPRoadmap, Data Stewardship Wizard, RDMO, EasyDMP, ezDMP, OpenDMP, etc.) and the convergence of funder requirements, common DMP themes, and emerging standards. Its main automation-relevant thread is machine-actionable DMPs (maDMPs): the RDA Common Standards working group's common data model and prototype workflows that let DMPs be exchanged and automatically assessed by connecting them to CRIS, repository, and funder systems, enabling automated FAIRness feedback. It situates DMP planning within the FAIR tools ecosystem and discusses workforce training, concluding that standardization and machine-actionability (not a single tool/template) are the path to interoperability.

title: Automated metadata annotation: What is and is not possible with machine learning
summary: This paper reviews the current state of automated metadata annotation using machine learning for cultural heritage and research data, arguing that annotation quality is bounded by the availability and homogeneity of domain training data. It draws challenges from use cases (scholarly/historical content is rarely available in consumable, interoperable, large-volume formats, unlike science/medicine) and proposes solutions to extend ML-based metadata generation. The work is a state-of-the-art assessment of what is and is not feasible with ML for metadata, rather than a single new system.

title: Microsoft Academic Graph: When experts are not enough
summary: The paper describes Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG), a heterogeneous knowledge graph built by AI software agents that crawl the public web and use NLP/semantic reasoning to read scholarly publications, then automatically disambiguate and link authors, institutions, venues, and concepts with minimal human effort. It argues machine curation reaches comparable or better accuracy than human-expert curation while being far more scalable and cheaper (updating MAG costs roughly one data scientist's salary), and introduces a reinforcement-learning-based 'saliency' eigencentrality measure plus PCA filtering to mitigate sampling biases, citation spam, and predatory venues. The work positions automated data curation as a remedy for the incompleteness and human biases that plague commercial curated databases like Clarivate.

title: ROBOT: A Tool for Automating Ontology Workflows
summary: ROBOT is an open-source Java library and command-line tool that packages low-level OWL API functionality into high-level operations for automating ontology development tasks in the OBO biomedical-ontology community. It automates format conversion, automated reasoning/logical validation, module/import extraction, merging, SPARQL-based querying, configurable quality-control reporting, repair, and templated term generation, which can be chained or orchestrated via GNU Make and CI (Travis) into reproducible release pipelines. It addresses the metadata/data-quality and provenance side of life-science data management, standardizing ontology curation so released artifacts are logically coherent and pass standard QC checks.

title: ODMedit: uniform semantic annotation for data integration in medicine based on a public metadata repository
summary: ODMedit is a web-based tool (built in R/FastRWeb over a MySQL metadata repository) that supports uniform semantic annotation of clinical/medical data elements to enable cross-source data integration. It uses a semi-automatic workflow: candidate UMLS codes from a large public metadata repository (portal of medical data models) are proposed and re-used, but a human expert makes every final coding decision. The authors explicitly note fully automated coding is not yet reliable, positioning this as expert-based annotation rather than agentic automation.

title: FAIRness through automation: development of an automated medical data integration infrastructure for FAIR health data in a maximum care university hospital
summary: The paper describes UMG-MeDIC, a microservices-based, fully open-source framework that automates the entire data-management lifecycle (ingest from heterogeneous hospital systems, pseudonymization, harmonization, ETL into a data warehouse, and curation for research) to make routine clinical data FAIR. Workflows are orchestrated by ActiveWorkflow 'agents' (Docker Agent, Annotation Agent, monitoring/validation service) that run containerized Python ETL jobs and capture Schema.org/JSON-LD process metadata in CouchDB for provenance and reproducibility. It is a real production deployment at a maximum-care university hospital, with emphasis on traceability, validation, and data-protection-compliant network zones.

title: DCSO: towards an ontology for machine-actionable data management plans
summary: This paper presents the DMP Common Standard Ontology (DCSO), a semantic (OWL/RDF/Turtle) serialisation of the RDA DMP Common Standard for representing machine-actionable Data Management Plans (maDMPs), plus a ShEx-based validation layer and a DCSX extension for controlled vocabularies. It documents the iterative creation process across versions 2.0.2 to 4.0.0 and a real-world use case integrating DCSO into the Data Stewardship Wizard (DSW) DMP-creation tool. The goal is to let automated systems both consume and produce maDMPs, reducing the administrative burden of DM planning and advancing FAIR compliance.

title: Data management plans as linked open data: exploiting ARGOS FAIR and machine actionable outputs in the OpenAIRE research graph
summary: This paper describes how the ARGOS/OpenDMP tool produces machine-actionable Data Management Plans (ma-DMPs) and integrates them as first-class FAIR entities into the OpenAIRE Research Graph, an Open Science knowledge graph. The work centers on a comparative mapping of three schemas (ARGOS/OpenDMP, OpenAIRE RG, and the RDA DMP Common Standard), plus export-format converters and semantic tagging that automate validation and exposure of DMPs linked to datasets, projects, funders, and publications. It is presented as the first effort to expose ma-DMPs in Open Science Graphs, advancing FAIRness and machine-actionable interlinking of research-process metadata.

title: Operationalizing and automating Data Governance
summary: Nadal et al. propose a framework that both operationalizes data governance (via a zoned Data Lake: Landing, Formatted, Exploitation zones with Data Governance Processes) and automates it through a concise set of metadata artifacts (physical, domain-independent, domain-specific) that drive auto-generated Data Collectors, Persistence Loaders, and Data Formatters. Given source metadata and schemas, the system automatically ingests, parses, and integrates heterogeneous structured and semi-structured data into a unified relational/analytics-ready form. The approach is demonstrated on a real WHO collaboration (WISCENTD) managing Neglected Tropical Disease data from internal (WIDP, WIMEDS) and external (UN) sources.

title: Data extraction methods for systematic review (semi)automation: Update of a living systematic review
summary: This living systematic review surveys 117 published NLP/ML/LLM methods and tools for (semi)automating data extraction from clinical study reports to support systematic reviewing, classifying their system architectures, evaluation metrics, data targets (mostly PICO entities), and reporting quality. The 2024 update finds large language models emerging as a new extraction tool, but warns that LLM-based work shows decreasing quality of quantitative results reporting (recall) and lower reproducibility, while trends toward relation extraction and code/dataset sharing continued. It is a benchmark/survey of automated data curation/extraction systems rather than a new agent system itself.

title: Concepção de uma Ferramenta Brasileira de Elaboração de Planos de Gestão de Dados de Pesquisa: desafios rumo ao modelo de planos acionáveis por máquina – MaDMP
summary: A Portuguese-language experience report on designing a conceptual model for a Brazilian research Data Management Plan tool, led by IBICT, aimed at the machine-actionable DMP (maDMP) model. Using Design Science Research, the authors compare existing DMP tools and conclude that customizing the existing DMPTool is the most viable path, with the IBICT tool serving as a central aggregator of information across the Brazilian science ecosystem. The 'agents' referenced are stakeholders in the research ecosystem rather than AI agents.

title: Ten principles for machine-actionable data management plans
summary: This PLoS Computational Biology education paper proposes 10 principles for making data management plans (DMPs) machine-actionable (maDMPs), shifting them from static free-text administrative documents into structured, living documents that systems can read, write, and act on. A central thrust (Principle 2) is allowing automated services to act on behalf of stakeholders for tasks like collating administrative data, cost estimation, license selection, storage booking, data deposit, and compliance validation, supported by common data models, PIDs, and controlled vocabularies. It is a community position/call-to-action paper grounded in RDA, FORCE11, and IDCC workshop consultations rather than an empirical system evaluation.

title: RDA DMP Common Standard for Machine-actionable Data Management Plans
summary: The RDA DMP Common Standard defines a common data model for machine-actionable Data Management Plans (maDMPs), specifying how DMP information can be represented in a structured, machine-readable form so it can be exchanged and acted upon automatically across tools and systems. It targets the data-management planning lifecycle stage, providing the enabling substrate on which automated maDMP tooling and services are built. It is a specification/standard rather than an AI agent or automation system itself, but it is the foundational infrastructure that maDMP automation depends on.

title: Towards Cognitive Automation of Data Science
summary: This 2015 AAAI paper proposes 'cognitive automation of data science,' aiming to automate the tedious end-to-end pipeline a data scientist runs: data ingestion, cleaning, and transformation (outlier removal, missing-value imputation), through model building, to presenting predictions aligned with user objectives. It targets the combinatorial explosion of algorithm/platform/parameter choices to speed time-to-results and open data science to non-experts. The data-management relevance is the early data-prep/quality stages, but the work is largely an AutoML-style automation effort rather than a dedicated data-management agent.

title: 304.1 Defining requirements for machine-actionable data management plans
summary: This RDA DMP Common Standards working group paper clarifies what machine-actionable Data Management Plans (maDMPs) are and defines an initial set of requirements and scope for a common data model, replacing free-form text DMPs to reduce researcher workload and bureaucracy. Using software/system requirements-engineering methodology and an open stakeholder consultation, it maps how different stakeholders' information needs evolve across phases of the research data lifecycle. It is a foundational, scope-defining contribution underpinning later automated/agentic DMP tooling rather than an implemented system.

title: DCSO: Towards an Ontology for Machine-actionable Data Management Plans
summary: The paper presents DCSO, an OWL/RDF ontology serialisation of the RDA DMP Common Standard application profile, designed to make Data Management Plans machine-actionable (maDMPs) so automated systems can consume and produce DMP content interoperably. It reuses established vocabularies (DCAT, Dublin Core, FOAF), adds a DCSX extension for controlled vocabularies (languages, countries, currencies), provides a ShEx validation layer for compliance checking, and demonstrates adoption via the Data Stewardship Wizard with JSON<->RDF (JSON-LD/Turtle) transformation. It is foundational standardization and tooling for automating the data-management-planning lifecycle stage rather than an autonomous AI agent.

title: Data trajectories: tracking reuse of published data for transitive credit attribution
summary: This 2016 paper introduces Data Trajectories (DTs), provenance graphs grounded in the W3C PROV model that capture how, by whom, and in what context a published dataset is reused across generations. It uses these graphs to automatically propagate a fraction of credit back to original data contributors and demonstrates the model via a Data Reuse Simulator. The work targets the provenance/lineage stage of the data lifecycle, automating transitive credit attribution to incentivize open data publication.

title: Next-Generation Data Management Plans: Global, Machine-Actionable, FAIR
summary: A progress report from the DCC and UC3/CDL on merging their DMPonline and DMPTool platforms into a shared infrastructure, with a roadmap toward machine-actionable, FAIR data management plans (maDMPs). The focus is making DMPs a more useful, globally interoperable exercise by implementing use cases that let DMP content be processed automatically rather than as static documents.

title: Information Integration for Machine Actionable Data Management Plans
summary: The paper argues that free-form data management plans fall short of supporting reproducibility and reuse, and proposes machine-actionable DMPs whose sections are auto-populated with information drawn from existing tools across digital preservation, reproducible research, open science, and data repositories. It maps those tools to standard DMP sections and proposes an ontology-based, standards-aligned data model enabling automated information integration. It identifies requirements and limitations of such a solution rather than evaluating a deployed system.

title: A Framework for the Preservation of a Docker Container
summary: This paper presents a framework and automated pipeline for preserving Docker containers to support reproducibility: a domain-specific language derived from a subset of the Dockerfile spec checks that a Dockerfile conforms to a model and extracts Docker/OS/package-version details. The build process is captured into the W3C PROV ontology to provide traceability and support citation and open science. It is rule-based automation for digital curation/preservation and provenance, not an AI-agent system.

title: A Landscape Survey of ActiveDMPs
summary: This 2018 survey reviews the emerging landscape of machine-actionable ('active') Data Management Plans (maDMPs), which aim to turn DMPs from an administrative burden into a useful, automatable artifact that connects researchers with service providers. It catalogs international fora, user-requirement gathering efforts, and DMP platforms in active development, and outlines a vision for making DMPs interoperable and machine-actionable. It concludes with next steps focused on connecting stakeholders and experimenting toward realizing maDMPs.

title: Engineering a machine learning pipeline for automating metadata extraction from longitudinal survey questionnaires
summary: This paper engineers a supervised machine-learning pipeline that automates the extraction of questionnaire metadata (questions, response domains, instructions, conditionals, etc.) from longitudinal-survey PDFs into DDI-Lifecycle-compliant items, using CLOSER Discovery as the train/test corpus. The pipeline frames extraction as a text-classification problem and wraps it in a reproducible engineering stack (Git for code, DVC for data/model versioning, and ProvLake for ML provenance logging) that tracks combinations of input data, models, and hyperparameters against evaluation metrics. The work emphasizes scalable metadata annotation/uplift and transparent, provenanced experiment management rather than a single best model.

title: Developing maDMPS-Centered Workflows and Automations to Streamline Processes: University of Colorado Boulder Case Study
summary: A University of Colorado Boulder case study, part of the IMLS-funded MAP pilot (California Digital Library + ARL), exploring how machine-actionable data management plans (maDMPs) can drive infrastructure planning, automate research-support workflows, and connect research data systems across campus. The team worked with campus stakeholders to evaluate existing tools, map integration opportunities, and identify scalable automation strategies, with emphasis on post-award data workflows. It is a workflow/automation effort centered on maDMP tooling rather than an AI-agent system per se.

title: DMP Notification for Efficiency and Coordination: University of California, Riverside Case Study
summary: This UC Riverside case study, part of the IMLS-funded MAP pilot run by the California Digital Library and ARL, explored AI-driven automation for campus computational resource deployment using the machine-actionable data-management plan (maDMP) as the central reference for researchers' resource needs. The team also tested workflows to simplify moving data between repositories by enabling cloud storage re-provisioning and managing HPC clusters. It is a real institutional pilot connecting maDMP metadata to automated planning, storage, and compute provisioning across the data lifecycle.

title: maDMPs Pilot Report
summary: The MAP (Machine Actionable Plans) Pilot, a CDL/ARL partnership funded by IMLS, gave academic libraries resources to explore machine-actionable data-management plans (maDMPs) and integrate them with existing research and IT systems to meet growing data-sharing requirements. The 28-page report covers project background, pilot activities, DMP Tool development, observations, and key recommendations for institutions adopting maDMPs. It targets the planning stage of the data-management lifecycle, emphasizing automation/interoperability of DMPs rather than purely manual documents.

title: Beyond ETL: How AI Agents Are Building Self-Healing Data Pipelines
summary: A conceptual review arguing that AI agents transform traditional ETL into self-healing data pipelines via a layered architecture of horizontal (cross-pipeline) and vertical (domain-specific) agents that perform proactive anomaly/drift detection, autonomous remediation (self-correction, dynamic rerouting, intelligent retry, fallback), and continuous learning. It also covers AI-driven data and metadata extraction (adaptive connectors, format recognition, auto-discovery, relationship/lineage mapping, schema inference) and cites industry case studies on downtime, compliance, and cost benefits. The piece is industry-oriented and synthesizes cited statistics rather than presenting original experiments.

title: Sysrev: A FAIR Platform for Data Curation and Systematic Evidence Review
summary: Sysrev is a free FAIR-motivated web platform for data curation and systematic evidence review, where users upload documents, define structured labels, recruit reviewers, and extract data, while machine learning models (trained per project via active learning) help prioritize and replicate reviewer decisions.
